Ash hauled Mr. Elm through the warehouse doors, lay him down on the cold concrete ramp, and cradling his blood-soaked head, swore through gritted teeth that he wasn't going to die today. Elm screamed, clutching his torn stomach. 

Hours earlier, before the bleeding began, undercover officer Danny Roarke had sat in a bare police safe room with his handler, Pruitt. Over and over, Pruitt forced him to rehearse a fabricated story about a drug bust in a public toilet involving four dogs, shaping the lie until Danny ceased reciting it and truly remembered it as his own past. He took that rehearsed memory into a dimly lit bar, performed it flawlessly for Bram, his son Cal, and Ash, earning a nod from the old boss and a place on the crew under a colour-free code name.

Now, inside the echoing hideout, Mr. Birch burst through the side entrance, furious and breathing hard. Birch argued bitterly that the robbery had been a setup from the start, insisted an informer had tipped off the police, and slipped back outside to bury the haul of diamonds where no watching eyes could find them.

Before the heist, Ren Vasco had walked straight out of a long prison sentence without ever speaking a word to the authorities. Reporting to Bram and Cal, who owed him dearly for his silence, Vasco was rewarded with an envelope and the alias Mr. Cedar. The next morning, eight men in matching black suits sat around a diner table, fiercely debating what a pop song was really about and whether waitresses deserved tips. Afterward, Bram dealt out tree aliases in his office, shushing Birch when he loudly complained that his name was the worst of the bunch.

The warehouse door rolled up, interrupting the present silence. Mr. Cedar strolled in, unhurried, and popped the boot of his car to drag out a bound, terrified patrolman named Doyle. Left alone with the captive, Cedar tuned a portable radio to an oldie, danced a light step, and sliced off Doyle’s ear with a razor before dousing the screaming officer in petrol. 

Earlier that afternoon, the heist had collapsed within sixty seconds. The alarm shrieked, and Ash had to shoot his way clear of the police from the getaway car, firing straight through the glass while Elm fled on foot. Scrambling down a residential street, Elm had tried to hijack a sedan, only for the terrified female driver to pull a pistol from her door pocket and shoot him in the stomach. Elm shot her dead, staggering back to Ash with a wound he could never explain away.

From the warehouse floor, watching Cedar flick a lighter over the petrol-drenched officer, Elm pulled his revolver and emptied it into Cedar, dropping him dead. Dragging himself closer, Elm whispered to the mutilated Doyle that he was an undercover cop and that a police force was already waiting outside for Bram to arrive. But when Cal walked in, he absorbed Elm’s altered account of Cedar’s betrayal, nodded grimly, and put three bullets into Doyle's chest to close the leak forever.

Moments later, Bram stepped into the warehouse. He looked down at the bodies, pointed a finger at the gut-shot Elm, and flatly named him as the police informer. Ash gasped, refused to believe his boss, and raised his gun directly at Bram to protect the man he had carried inside. 

Guns roared in the enclosed space. When the smoke cleared, Bram and Cal lay dead, and Ash slumped against the wall, mortally wounded beside Elm. 

Bleeding out on the floor, Elm looked up into Ash’s dying eyes and gave him the truth, confessing that he was indeed a police officer. Ash stared in agonizing betrayal, raised his barrel, and shot Elm through the head just as the warehouse doors blew open and SWAT officers swarmed the room, cutting Ash down in a hail of gunfire.

I. THE WATCH

In a bare front room, a returning prisoner of war sat a young boy down and placed in his hands the gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of captivity. 

Years later, sitting in a motel room on the edge of town, that same boy, Denny, asked his girlfriend Marielle if she had remembered to pack it. She had not; it still lay on the bedside table of his watched flat. Denny drove back into the city, let himself inside, and reclaimed the watch. When a hitman emerged from the bathroom, Denny reached the submachine gun resting on the kitchen counter first, shooting Rollo dead. Hours later, with the gold watch secured back around his wrist, Denny picked up Marielle and rode out of the city on a borrowed motorcycle.

II. THE BRIEFCASE

Hitmen Rollo and Marcus drove across the city debating European drug laws and foreign names for fast food. Waiting in a corridor outside a target's flat, they argued whether giving a foot massage justified being thrown from a balcony. Inside, Marcus recited scripture, shot young Tobin for skimming from their employer Otis, and seized a leather briefcase. A fourth man burst from the bathroom, emptying a revolver at them point-blank; every shot missed, a miracle Marcus took as a sign to quit the life. 

In the car afterward, Rollo’s gun accidentally discharged over a bump, blowing off passenger Del’s head and spraying the interior with blood. Marcus pulled into his friend Warren’s garage, where a soft-spoken fixer timed a total cleanup, hosing the men down and dressing them in borrowed shorts and T-shirts. Wearing these ridiculous clothes, they delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar. Otis barely looked up from counting out cash to Denny, an ageing boxer he was paying to take a dive in the fifth round. 

Afterward, over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner. When they drawn their gun on the patrons, Marcus calmly talked the gunman down, surrendered his wallet, recited his passage of scripture once more, kept the briefcase, and allowed the couple to walk free.

III. THE POWDER AND THE BLADES

Rollo bought a bag of unusually pure heroin from his dealer Kip, shooting up at the kitchen table before taking Otis’s wife, Nadia, to a themed restaurant where they danced barefoot and won a contest. Returning home, Nadia mistook the heroin in Rollo’s coat for cocaine and snorted a line. She collapsed, turning blue, until Rollo rushed her back to Kip's living room and revived her with a syringe of adrenaline plunged straight into her heart.

That same night at the arena, Denny broke his promise to Otis. He refused to go down in the fifth, hitting his opponent so hard the man died in the ring. Denny escaped in a taxi before the crowd realized what had happened. 

After killing Rollo in his flat, Denny sped away, only to collide with Otis crossing the street with a paper bag in his arms. Both men wrecked their vehicles and, bruised and disoriented, were dragged into a pawnshop basement by a pair of sadistic captors. Denny managed to break free from his bonds and reached the street door. Hearing Otis being assaulted below, Denny paused, pulled a steel sword down off the shop wall, and descended back into the cellar to save his former boss. Standing over their dead captors, Otis declared them square—on the single condition that Denny left the city and never returned.

At the end of the rail line, Tobias met Ivy on a cold beach full of strangers, breaking a window into an empty shore house where they slept on the floorboards. Over two years, love built itself across frozen river ice, noodle house windows blurred with steam, and silent drive-in backseats. Then the same rooms turned sour; her drinking met his tight-lipped withholding, each knowing exactly which words wounded deepest. It ended at two in the morning when she came home having dented his car, their row escalating until she took a bag and walked out forever.

On a Tuesday morning, Tobias skipped work on an impulse he could not explain. He took the train to the coast, stepped onto the frozen sand, and found a woman with dyed hair standing near the surf as if waiting for him.

After leaving him, Ivy paid a shabby clinic to erase Tobias entirely from her head. Days later, Tobias visited her bookshop to reconcile, only to be met by her distant, polite gaze as she flirted with a young clerk named Peck. Devastated, Tobias was shown the clinic’s form letter by his friends Nina and Grady. He marched into the office of Dr. Hallam, demanding the exact same treatment, and filled two carrier bags with every keepsake—a hairslide, a mug, a torn page—so the machine could map her out of his brain.

They drove back to the city talking as easily as old friends. Outside her apartment building, Ivy invited Tobias inside for a drink, neither able to account for the immediate, uncanny comfort between them.

That night, technicians Dell and Peck attached the cap to Tobias’s sleeping head. Peck quietly pocketed the bag of mementos to use on Ivy himself. Inside his own mind, Tobias watched the worst, final fights dissolve into nothingness. But when the deletion reached the moments he cherished, panic struck; he tried to smuggle Ivy into safe corners of his memory where she had never been, like a childhood kitchen. Outside, Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on Tobias’s bed, completely missing that the map on their screens had gone wildly off course.

At the clinic, Rosa abruptly quit her job. In a final act of defiance, she emptied the filing cabinets and mailed the original session tapes and case files back to every patient on the registry.

Dr. Hallam was summoned at three in the morning to stabilize Tobias's process. In the hallway, Rosa impulsively kissed Hallam, only for Hallam's arriving wife to inform Rosa that her own past affair with the doctor had been systematically erased from her mind. Hallam restored the map, driving Tobias down to his very last surviving memory: the night in the shore house. There, as the walls crumbled around them, Ivy's memory urged him to meet her at the beach. When the machine finished before dawn, Tobias woke up with a headache and a strange flatness, unaware she had ever existed.

Two envelopes arrived in Ivy’s building. Sitting side by side in the stairwell, Tobias and Ivy clicked play on the cassette player, listening to their own recorded voices viciously tearing each other apart. Horrified by the venom of their past, Ivy bolted down the stairs. But at the front entrance she paused, turned around, and walked back up to sit beside him, where they agreed to try again anyway.

In the dim glow of a screening room, the reporter Nash watched the nine-minute newsreel obituary summarizing the public life of Emmett Rusk. The flickering film recapped how Emmett, upon turning twenty-five and seizing his immense inheritance, spitefully selected a failing city newspaper, the Clarion, as his plaything. The screen showed his early days sleeping at the office alongside his manager Marsh and friend Devlin above a printed front-page declaration of principles, followed by his extravagant buyout of a rival paper’s staff celebrated with brass bands and chorus lines. It chronicled his marriage to Adele, the governor’s niece, and the silent breakfast tables that heralded their decay; his secret affair with shopgirl Nora Kell after a splashed coat; party boss Halloran exposing the affair mid-campaign; Emmett’s refusal to withdraw, leading to election loss, Devlin’s transfer request, and divorce; his second marriage to Nora and forced opera campaign; Nora’s humiliating debut, completed in print by Emmett himself after firing a drunk Devlin; her suicide attempt by poison that finally halted her singing; her retreat into the vast halls of Silvermount working jigsaw puzzles; their bitter beach picnic dispute before she left him; his frantic destruction of her bedroom where he found a snow globe and whispered a single unknown word; and finally his solitary death in his unfinished palace, where he uttered "Bluebell" once more, dropped the glass sphere to break on the floor, and left the world bewildered.

Years before any of those grand failures, in the drafty kitchen of a Western mining boarding house, Emmett’s mother had sat across from the eastern banker Barrow. A defaulted lodger’s seemingly worthless mine deed had struck an enormous seam, transforming the family’s fortunes overnight. Ignoring her husband’s quiet protests from the doorway, she signed her young son and the sudden riches over to the banker, convinced it was the only way to buy him a grander life. Outside in the snow, the young boy lashed out against his fate, driving his wooden sled violently into Barrow’s stomach and knocking the banker down, only to be hauled away toward the east before the evening fell.

In a seaside nightclub at four in the afternoon, Nash tracked down Nora. She sat hunched over a drink, bleary-eyed and furious, and slammed her glass on the table, barking at him to get out before he could even finish asking his question about her dead husband’s final word.

Nash turned instead to historical records and surviving associates. In a grand marble library, he pored over Barrow’s published memoirs, reading the dead banker’s bitter account of Emmett’s stubborn rise. He interviewed Marsh in his quiet office, sought out Devlin in self-imposed exile, and spoke with Colm, the loyal old butler who had tended Silvermount’s cold corridors during Emmett’s final years. 

Standing in the cavernous Great Hall of Silvermount among unpacked crates and echoey marble, Nash snapped his notebook shut. He told Colm and the remaining house staff that his search was over, reasoning that no single, simple word could ever hope to explain the vast, contradictory span of a man's life. He walked out into the cold afternoon, completely unaware that down in the basement, workmen clearing out the palace's accumulated junk were lifting a small, battered child's sled, painted with the faded name Bluebell, and shoveling it directly into the roar of the furnace.

Behind an insurance desk, Martin Kray systematically refused Elias Prine’s claim, writing off the man’s post-traumatic memory loss as purely psychosomatic. Unable to believe her husband’s condition was real, Prine’s diabetic wife tested him by asking for injection after injection, dying of an overdose he gave her without any memory of the previous doses.

At a dimly lit bar, a woman named Corinne watched a stranger walk in wearing her missing boyfriend Gil’s suit and park Gil’s sports car outside. Smiling brightly behind the counter, she served Martin a pint of beer her staff had quietly spat in.

Months after the Prine claim, two intruders shattered the glass of Martin’s bathroom door at night. Martin shot one dead across his wife’s body before the second smashed his head into the mirror, wiping away his ability to forge new memories. Desperate to tether himself to reality, Martin constructed a rigid filing system of Polaroid photographs, captioned notes, and tattoos, though when he burned his wife’s hairbrush and books in an open field, he could not hold the grief long enough to mourn her.

Corinne hid every pen in her house, goaded Martin until he struck her, and returned bruised to blame a man named Vance. Guided by her lie, Martin waited in the dark of a motel bathroom, beat Vance senseless as he walked through the door, and drove him out of town at gunpoint.

Sitting on a motel bed he did not remember booking, Martin recited the Prine file into a telephone receiver to an anonymous caller who fed him a drug dealer’s name and address. Martin cornered Gil Marsh in a flooded basement, throttled him with a leather belt, and took a photo of the corpse. As Gil died, he whispered "Elias"—a word Martin could not explain before putting on the dead man's clothes and taking his keys.

Corinne found the licence plate scribbled on a stray note in Martin's pocket, ran the registration through a contact at the vehicle registry, and handed Martin an official paper bearing the name Roy Mercer.

In a derelict building out past the town line, a plainclothes officer named Roy sat Martin down and exposed the entire tragic illusion. Roy had helped Martin track down and kill his wife’s true attacker a year ago—a vengeance Martin forgot within minutes. Gil had been innocent, the telephone calls were Roy’s way of giving Martin an ongoing purpose, and the helpless man in the Prine story was Martin himself. Refusing to accept a reality that left him empty, Martin burned the photos of Gil, wrote *HE IS LYING TO YOU* across Roy’s picture, copied Roy’s licence plate as his next target, and had the registration inked onto his thigh as his sixth permanent fact.

Trusting the tattoo inked into his own flesh, Martin lured Roy back to that same derelict building under a fake pretext. He walked the officer into the shadowed room, put a bullet straight through his head, and photographed the corpse, entirely satisfied that his system had delivered justice once again.

An ex-convict named Wes Tarrow, newly born again with scripture inked up both forearms, holds down a job and coaches a boys' baseball team on Saturdays. His wife Nita watches his absolute certainty with quiet dread, fearing his fanaticism and his temper in equal measure. A pickup truck comes through a road crossing at the wrong moment and strikes Lena Ward’s husband Doug and their two young daughters. The truck goes on a hundred yards, stops with the engine idling, backs up a little, and then flees. Wes walks up the steps of a police station, confesses to the hit-and-run at the counter, and is sent back to prison. Released early on a recommendation, Wes walks past Nita waiting at the gate, abandoning his family and his faith to take work cleaning rooms at a roadside motel far from home. After everything, wounded and bleeding through his shirt, he goes home to his family.

Four adults, a baby, and a rottweiler named Tigre shared a house built for two. Ruben slept on the couch, watching his brother Nestor’s wife, Alma, move through the kitchen. When Nestor came home from robbing a pharmacy and knocked Alma across the room, Ruben urged her to run away with him. Knowing Tigre killed other dogs on sight, Ruben entered him in local dogfights, steadily stashing his winnings. Desperate to free Alma, Ruben paid two thugs to beat Nestor. But Nestor recovered, deduced Ruben’s hand in it, stole Ruben’s hidden savings, and fled with Alma and the baby. Out of money, Ruben took Tigre to one last fight. When the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring, Ruben stabbed Chaco, grabbed the dog, and fled in a truck with his friend Pipo. Desperate and speeding, Ruben ran a red light and ploughed into a turning car. Months later, Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank. At the funeral, Ruben made one final plea to Alma, but she refused him for good.

The model Celine Vaz lived inside her own image after her lover Hector walked out on his wife and daughters, moving Celine into a new flat directly facing her own billboard. Then came the collision at the junction: Ruben’s speeding truck tore into Celine’s car. She woke in a hospital ward with steel pins holding her shattered leg together, terrified for her lapdog, Chispa, who had been left alone. Back in the flat, Chispa had fallen through a hole in the floorboards and could not escape. As Hector systematically tore up the floor with a crowbar searching for the whining animal, Celine’s untended leg turned gangrenous. Surgeons amputated her leg above the knee. That same week, workers stripped down her giant billboard, leaving Celine and Hector sitting in a ruined flat, staring out at a blank frame.

Cardo, a former guerrilla turned vagrant hitman, was pushing his scrap cart through the junction when the crash occurred. As smoke rose from the wreckage, he pulled the bleeding rottweiler from the back seat and walked away. Over weeks, Cardo nursed Tigre back to health among his yard of strays. The man was no stranger to violence: a businessman named Elian had hired him to murder his partner and half-brother, Sergio. Shortly after, Cardo stood far back at his estranged wife’s burial before following his grown daughter, Perla, home. One evening, Cardo returned to his yard to find Tigre had slaughtered every stray in the pack. Cardo pressed a gun against the dog's head, but could not pull the trigger. Instead of killing Sergio as contracted, Cardo abducted him and chained him to a bed frame in the yard. He then brought Elian face to face with Sergio, laid a loaded pistol on the floor between the brothers, collected money from both, and walked out. Cardo broke into Perla’s flat while she was out, left a lengthy confession on her answering machine detailing who he was and why he had disappeared, and took her photograph off the shelf. Shaved and dressed in clean clothes, he left his earnings on her table and walked out into the flat grey wasteland, Tigre trotting at his side.

Above the blue light flooding the pavement, an old man stood at an open flat window explaining to a younger man that nothing anybody made or loved ever survived time. It was not a complaint, he remarked softly into the cool night air, but simply an iron fact of the world.

On the street below, police officers hauled Cort and Jonah out through the parted crowd, their hands pinned in steel behind their backs. One man was shouting uselessly against the sirens while the other hung his head in absolute silence, swept into the back of the waiting vans.

Minutes earlier, inside the basement club, Jonah had lifted a heavy red fire extinguisher and smashed it down into a man’s face, swinging again and again long after the body stopped moving on the stained concrete floor. A few feet away, blended quietly into the shadows of the watching crowd, the real Adder stood with his arms folded, watching the bloody mistake unfold.

Before the extinguisher fell, Cort had hunted frantic through the low-ceilinged gloom, pulling faces into the dim light until he grabbed the wrong man by the collar. The stranger had instantly seized Cort’s forearm at the elbow and twisted it with cold precision until the bone snapped inside the sleeve.

Earlier that night, two men had detached themselves from a dark alleyway doorway and offered Cort a name and a location for a handful of crumpled banknotes. They had pointed down the damp asphalt toward the basement entrance of the Pit, steering the desperate pair straight into the dark.

Before they ever bought that name, Cort and Jonah had stumbled out of the flat party still half-laughing, only to freeze on the pavement. In front of them, paramedics were quietly securing a blanket around a gurney and loading a bruised, familiar face into the back of an ambulance.

Before the ambulance arrived, the Adder had forced Lise down onto the concrete of the pedestrian underpass. He raped her with brutal indifference and pounded her head against the floor while a solitary late-night pedestrian peeked around the corner, caught her eyes for a terrible second, and backed away into the dark.

Lise had descended into that underpass only to avoid crossing four lanes of blinding headlights above. Halfway along the tiled corridor, she had walked directly in on the Adder, who had a transsexual woman by the hair and was explaining something to her with his fist.

Hours before the underpass, Cort had grown belligerent, high, and sloppy at the flat party, openly pursuing other women across the crowded room. Lise had watched him for twenty minutes in quiet disgust before pulling her coat from the bedroom bed and stepping out into the cold on her own.

Earlier that evening, Lise, Cort, and Jonah had stood swaying together in a noisy underground carriage. They had argued cheerfully about sex and how much Cort had already managed to drink before nine o'clock, tossing banter back and forth with the unthinking confidence of people who fully expected to be doing the exact same thing tomorrow.

Earlier that afternoon, the sun had been warm over the public park. Sprinklers turned slow circles over freshly cut grass, spraying mist over playing children, while Lise lay on her side in the turf with an unopened book, resting one flat palm gently against her lower stomach.

Before the park, Lise had sat completely alone on the edge of the bath in the quiet flat. She had held the white plastic stick in both hands, watching the second line darken, and allowed herself a solitary smile before she told anyone at all.

And earlier still, in the morning light filtered through thin bedroom curtains, Lise lay tangled in the sheets beside Cort. She described a recurring dream of a long red tunnel that kept frightening her, while the two of them traded lazy insults about Jonah, her ex-boyfriend who was now just the friend they both shared.

In the stifling heat of a glass-countered shop, Nadir stood beside his grown daughter, Sahar, who translated as the dealer openly mocked the accent of the man buying a handgun. 

Across town outside a restaurant, Trey and Kwame drew pistols on prosecutor Halstead and his wife Paula, taking their luxury car off the kerb. 

Later that night, on a deserted country stretch, Officer Voss would pull his cruiser over to offer a ride to a young hitchhiker walking through the rain. As the young man reached into his coat pocket for a cigarette, Voss would panic, fire two fatal rounds into his chest, drive the body into a ditch, and ignite the car to erase the evidence.

Before that fatal rain fell, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart on a dark road. Boyle made Clay stand three feet away while he groped Renee beneath her skirt. The next morning, Boyle’s partner, Voss, asked their commander for a new patrol car, taking a reassignment lie about flatulence just to escape riding with a racist.

At the Halstead residence, locksmith Mateo changed the front door locks while Paula stood above him on the stairs, declaring loudly to her husband that the tattooed worker would sell their keys to criminals. Mateo moved on to Nadir’s retail store, fitting a new lock but warning Nadir that the door frame itself was rotted through. Nadir, suspecting a con to wring more money from him, ordered Mateo out.

Desperate for his father’s failing health, Boyle sat in an insurance office pleading with a clerk named Delia Frank, only to be flatly denied treatment and ejected after exploding in rage at her badge. 

Night came, and Nadir’s shop was smashed open—the broken door yielding exactly as Mateo had warned. The insurer reviewed the claim and refused to pay a dime because Nadir had ignored the structural warning. 

On a freeway slip road, a car flipped and caught fire. Renee Hobart was trapped upside down in the burning wreck until Boyle crawled through the smashed window, sliced her seatbelt, and dragged her clear of the flames.

Elsewhere, Trey and Kwame hit a small man named Pham with their stolen car, folded him across the bonnet, argued for two streets, and dumped his breathing body outside a hospital entrance. 

When police later surrounded Clay Hobart in his own car, believing it stolen, Clay refused to submit. Four officers raised their weapons, but Voss stepped between them, de-escalating the standoff and driving Clay safely home. Clay then sped away with Trey cowering in his passenger seat, finally pulling onto a dark highway verge to toss the youth out into the night.

Consuming himself with fury over his ruined business, Nadir waited outside Mateo’s house with his new pistol. As Mateo stepped onto the pavement, his small daughter Rosie ran into his arms. Nadir shouted and pulled the trigger. Nothing happened; Sahar had secretly loaded the gun with blanks. Seeing the child unharmed, Nadir dropped to his knees, convinced an angel had intervened.

Then the rain began to fall on the dark country road. Voss pulled his patrol car alongside Kwame, who was hitchhiking alone. They talked briefly before Kwame reached into his jacket pocket. Driven by sudden fear, Voss drew his weapon, shot Kwame dead, dumped his body in a muddy ditch, and set the cruiser ablaze.

Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the roadside the following morning. Approaching the body in the mud, he stopped cold, recognizing his brother Kwame’s shoes. At home, his mother collapsed onto the kitchen floor, weeping and blaming Reece for never going out to look for him.

In her empty house, Paula Halstead tripped at the top of her staircase and tumbled down. Lying injured on the floor, she clutched the arm of her housekeeper, Alba, telling the woman she was the only friend she had left in the world.

Having been abandoned on the highway, Trey bought Pham’s old garage van cheap. Opening the rear doors expecting auto parts, he discovered two dozen trafficked migrants sitting in the dark. Trey drove them to the docks, emptied his pockets into their hands, and set them free.

As the first snow of the year began to fall across the city, two cars touched bumper-to-bumper at a busy junction. Both drivers leapt out into the cold, shouting before either had even looked at the damage.

Helicopters roared low through the night, spraying chemical pesticide across every neighborhood roof to eradicate invasive crop pests. The following evening, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his artist wife, Bess, reluctantly readied their home for an unwanted dinner party. The next morning, baker Otto Kemp took an order for a young boy’s birthday cake, carefully writing down the name Charlie Rill. 

Later that afternoon, a hurried waitress named Rhona struck young Charlie with her car on his way to school; though knocked down, the boy stubbornly insisted he was unhurt and walked back home. Within hours, Charlie collapsed into a deep coma, leaving his frantic parents, Grant and Elaine, to maintain a desperate hospital vigil. As the silent hours dragged on, Grant’s estranged father Duff arrived unexpectedly in the corridor and clumsily confessed a decades-old extramarital affair. Meanwhile, angry about an unpaid, uncollected birthday cake, Otto began dialing the Rill household late at night, making menacing anonymous phone calls.

Across the city, telephone-sex worker Cheryl folded laundry while guiding clients through fantasies over her headset, all while her bitter husband, Stu, sat beside her on the couch seething in silence. Seeking escape, Stu and three friends drove out to the mountain streams to fish, only to discover a young woman’s body floating face down in the shallows. Unwilling to sacrifice their trip, the men tethered the corpse’s ankle to the riverbank with fishing line and carried on fishing for two full days before alerting anyone. When Vern returned home and recounted the weekend, his wife Iris, a party clown wiping off her makeup at the kitchen table, was filled with utter disgust.

Night after night, jazz singer Vida performed under low club lights while her cellist daughter, Bee, practiced alone in an empty house. Elsewhere, police officer Rowe, secretly cheating on his wife Peg with a woman named Nan, drove the family dog out to the valley and abandoned it on the roadside to cover one of his alibis. When Nan’s ex-husband Cass—a helicopter pilot—discovered she was seeing a new man, he burst into her house and methodically sawed all her furniture to pieces.

House-sitting at the Hartigans' residence, Ike and Dot passed the time by applying pale foundation and fake bruises, taking photographs of Dot posed as a beaten corpse in the hallway. At the Hartigan dinner party that evening, Bess blurted out an admission regarding a long-ago nude modeling session and an affair, causing Neil to erupt into a humiliating scene before their guests.

The following morning, Charlie died in the hospital ward. Driven by grief and anger over the harassment, Grant and Elaine went straight to the bakery to confront Otto; upon learning of the boy's death, the remorseful baker served them warm bread and wept with them. That afternoon, Bee returned home, found her mother Vida asleep in a chair, closed the garage door, and sat inside the running car until carbon monoxide ended her life. Later, during a hilltop picnic, Stu’s violent rage broke completely, and he picked up a heavy rock and smashed a young woman’s head.

Just before nightfall, a sudden tremor shook the entire city, rattling windows and shaking foundations. By nightfall, every death, every wreck, and every private ruin across the city were folded together into a single evening news bulletin.

For six months, I was an insomniac product-recall investigator who could only sleep after weeping at church support groups for diseases I did not have. Then Ada Vey started attending the same meetings. Her obvious, performative faking exposed my own lie, and my sleep vanished completely.

In a concrete service stairwell beneath a target tower, a man named Rex Marrow would beat me down a flight at a time. Deep in that future dark, I would realize the gun in his hand was held in my own grip, press the metal barrel into my cheek, and pull the trigger, the gunshot tearing through my flesh to destroy him once and for all.

Before that end, I sat on a business flight next to Rex Marrow, a soap salesman with bad luggage who ranted about modern life before handing me his card. When an explosion blew my flat and all my catalogue furniture onto the pavement, I stood at a phone box and called him. Rex took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district.

Outside a bar one night, Rex asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody in the car park until we were both laughing. That brawl hardened into a weekly basement club with its own strict rules, pulling in more and more members.

When Ada overdosed, Rex brought her back to the derelict house, starting a loud affair that echoed through the floors while I lay rigid downstairs. Rex kept busy, rendering fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap and selling it back to department stores at eighty dollars a bar. One afternoon, Rex poured wet lye onto the back of my hand, holding me to the table and refusing to let me retreat into meditation, scarring me forever.

I walked into my office and used my beaten face to blackmail my employer into paying me to stay away. With that income, Rex transformed the club into an organisation called Havoc. He filled the house with shaven recruits who slept on floors, took orders, and vandalized corporate property. During a heavy rain, Rex steered our car into oncoming traffic, let it roll into a ditch, and vanished.

When a recruit named Ogden was shot dead by police on an operation, I started trying to shut Havoc down. I travelled from city to city, only to find identical basement clubs everywhere. Barmen and desk clerks greeted me with the same name: Rex Marrow.

In a motel room with flight records spread over the bed, I worked out the truth. There was no separate salesman; Rex and I were the same person, acting while I slept. I called Ada on the telephone, and she confirmed she had been sleeping with me, not another man.

I tracked down Havoc’s ultimate target: vans packed with explosives in the car parks beneath the debt-record towers, set to wipe out everyone's financial history. I went down to defuse the charges, but Rex confronted me.

Just as I had foreseen, he dragged me down the concrete service stairwell. Understanding the truth, I put the gun in my own mouth and fired through my cheek, taking the wound to kill Rex forever.

Bleeding and wrapped in bandages, I stood at a high window as the shaven recruits brought Ada to the room, apologized, and left us alone. She took my hand, and together we watched from the window as the debt-record towers came down one after another.

Disguised as devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew robbed a diamond house in a northern port, walking out with an exceptionally massive stone. Overseas, his cousin Marv called immediately, instructing Solly to bring the diamond straight over to him. Back in the city underworld, Grigor the Nail told Solly about a lucrative bookmaker’s while simultaneously tipping off pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob him at that exact location.

Meanwhile, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. The deal turned violent, and Finn, a bare-knuckle fighter from the camp, knocked Sam out cold. This left Halloway without a contestant for gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout. Cornered, Halloway had to put Finn into the fight instead, promising Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city, delivered the stone to a fence named Hersch for safekeeping, and proceeded to the bookmaker’s to bet on the fight. Ike, Benno, and Tulley bungled the robbery, seizing Solly’s arm and his briefcase before Grigor chased them off. That night, Finn ruined the arrangement by knocking his opponent out cold in the very first round. Coldstone lost a fortune on his wagers and vented his rage on Halloway.

Marv flew in from overseas, found Solly gone, and hired the relentless bounty hunter Ledge to track him down. Grigor took Solly to an underworld workshop and severed his arm to open the briefcase, only to discover the stone was not inside. Ledge quickly traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took custody of both them and the stone.

Coldstone later disposed of Solly by feeding him to his pigs, using the horror to threaten Halloway and Digby with the same fate if the second fight went wrong. Halloway and Digby instructed Finn to go down in the fourth round, but Coldstone’s men escalated the feud by burning Finn’s mother to death in her caravan.

On a city road, Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car with Ike and Benno trapped inside. In the chaotic shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Amid the slaughter, Tulley escaped with a dog that had swallowed the loose diamond.

At the rematch, Finn waited until the agreed fourth round, only to knock his opponent out cold once again, while armed travellers hidden in the crowd massacred Coldstone’s men. Halloway and Digby found the isolated Coldstone and shot him dead, and by morning the travellers had completely vanished.

Finally, the dog was handed in at a pet shop, where it coughed up the diamond, leaving Halloway and Digby holding the priceless stone.

In a transparent zoo enclosure on a distant planet, he sat beside a famous film actress while green, saucer-shaped creatures observed them. The alien guides explained that every moment exists simultaneously, that free will is merely an illusion peculiar to Earth, and that death is only a single, unchanging point in an infinite tapestry.

In a small industrial town, he was born physically slight and peculiar. His father tossed him into the deep end of a municipal swimming pool to teach him to swim, but he simply sank to the bottom, floating in the quiet dark until hands dragged him up.

A bright beam weapon flashed across a crowded lecture hall, striking him dead after he addressed the audience about the death he had always known was coming. He fell to the stage, the fulfillment of a pledge made long ago by an avenging prisoner who had promised to orchestrate his murder on account of a dead scout.

On a reeking prison train, that scout died of gangrene in a crowded corner, using his final breath to blame him for his demise. The pair had been captured together after wandering lost through winter fields behind enemy lines, where the scout had repeatedly beaten him for wanting to be left behind in the snow to die.

Conscripted as a chaplain’s assistant, he was shipped overseas with no combat training worth mentioning. Following his capture, he was held in a prisoner-of-war camp beside enemy officers who spent years eating well, drawing double rations through a clerical error in the administrative ledger.

He sat before a studio microphone on a radio talk show, trying to tell the listening world about the fourth dimension, his abduction, and the aliens. His daughter heard the broadcast, decided he had become senile, and took his financial and legal affairs completely out of his hands.

He lay in a hospital bed after a sudden physical collapse, where another patient introduced him to the paperbacks of an obscure, prolific hack science fiction writer. 

In a great, ruined city, captors forced him and other prisoners into choked cellars to dig out corpses until one of the diggers died of the dry heaves. They had been housed beneath the city in a disused abattoir's underground meat locker. A firestorm destroyed the entire metropolis in a single night, and the prisoners emerged from the cold cellar in the morning to find the world above gone.

He married the daughter of the man who owned an optometry school and became rich. Later, he survived an air crash in the mountains, but his wife died of exhaust fumes in her car while driving frantically toward the hospital where he was brought.

No instant leads to another. He stands before the lecture audience. He sinks to the bottom of the pool. He listens to the alien guides in the zoo. He digs in the subterranean ash. He is born weak. He is shot dead. All moments exist at once.

Emlyn sat in Wilder’s armchair, entirely composed, and explained that he had known about the betrayal for four years. Odile had told him the full story during their trip abroad, he added smoothly, and in truth he had never thought much of Wilder’s romantic prose style in those intercepted letters anyway.

Earlier that same evening, Wilder had telephoned his oldest friend in a state of absolute panic, pleading with him to come over to his house without delay so they could finally speak.

Wilder had dialed the telephone only after Odile let slip a stray detail over their drinks in town: Emlyn had been quietly publishing a dreadful contemporary novelist whom Wilder represented, a hack writer both men had always quietly detested in private.

In a dimly lit bar two years after they had abandoned their hidden sanctuary, Odile had sat across from Wilder to break the news that her marriage was officially over. She explained with solemn satisfaction that she had spent the previous night confessing the entire history of their affair to her husband.

Before that evening in the bar, the physical reality of their affair had already withered away. Deciding that the domestic maintenance of their secret flat had turned into an onerous chore, Wilder and Odile had divided up their cheap crockery, packed away the linen, and surrendered the lease to the landlord.

Long before the lease was surrendered, all three had gathered in the married couple's home for dinner. Sitting at the head of the table, the two men had retreated into energetic, exclusionary banter about racquet games and forgotten schoolboy sport, driving the conversation so aggressively that Odile was left with no part in the talk at all.

Days before that dinner, Emlyn had sat through a long, drunken restaurant lunch with Wilder. He had spent the entire afternoon baiting the agent about the wretched state of contemporary fiction, lingering over his third bottle of wine while never once revealing the bitter knowledge he carried.

Odile had returned to the rented rooms straight from her travels, offering no details whatsoever about the trip abroad. She allowed the quiet afternoon to pass precisely as all the others had passed, preserving the comfortable illusion of an undisturbed secret.

Her silence concealed the confrontation in a hotel room overseas, where her husband’s persistent questioning had driven her to confess the affair entirely. Emlyn had absorbed the confession without visible anger, remarking coolly that he had always been far fonder of his friend than of his wife.

That confession had been triggered downstairs in the hotel lobby, when Emlyn had paused at the front desk to enquire about an envelope held under her name, carrying a handwritten address he recognized immediately.

Months before that journey, Odile had sat on the bed in their private flat to announce she was carrying her husband’s child. Neither lover suggested an ending to their arrangement; instead, they decided the rented rooms would continue exactly as before.

They had established that second household together in a quiet district, carefully stocking the cupboards with fresh linen and matching stacks of plates, endowing their affair with an ordinary domestic life of its own.

And before the quiet rooms, the pregnancy, and the years of silence, there had been a lively party in Emlyn’s home. While the rest of the guests drank and laughed downstairs, Wilder had led his best friend’s wife upstairs into a quiet bedroom, where he told her just how lovely she was.
